resources.string: Your phone turned into a simple seismograph

This app uses your phone accelerometer to measure the movement of a surface, such as a table. With the phone resting on it, it records how the surface moves and tells you how strong it was, how long it lasted and in which direction it happened.\n\nIt also draws the signal in real time and lets you save each measurement and export it as CSV to analyze in Excel.

In short:
1. Lay the phone flat on the table.
2. Calibrate with the table still.
3. Tap Measure and move the table.
4. Check the result and save it.

Tap How to use for the detailed guide.

With the filter on, the app smooths the signal and discards readings that cannot be told apart from the sensor noise, so the result reflects the real movement better. With the filter off you see the raw signal with all its noise: useful to study the sensor itself or to compare. The CSV records which one you used.

Automatic: the measurement starts when movement is detected and ends when the table is still again. Fixed time (1 to 60 s): measures exactly that long from when the movement starts. Use it to compare measurements of the same length or to capture a long movement.
The triangle marks where the peak of your measurement fell. The scale goes from almost none (green) to very strong (red).

How to read it: the curve rises when the movement is stronger. The movement lies between "start" and "end" and the dot marks the peak. Anything below the threshold line is not counted as movement: it is sensor noise.
Horizontal axis → Time in seconds (s). 0 is the instant the movement started; negative values are the rest before it started.
Vertical axis ↑ Total acceleration |a| in m/s²: how strong the movement is at each instant, combining the three axes.
Vertical axis ↑ Estimated velocity |v| in m/s: how fast the table moves.
Vertical axis ↑ Estimated displacement |d| in mm: how far the table moved from its starting position.
Vertical axis ↑ Acceleration of each phone axis in m/s². It can be positive or negative: the sign shows the direction of the movement.

Shows which way the table moved. x: to the right (+) or left (−) of the phone. y: toward the top (+) or bottom (−) of the phone, on the same surface. z: vertical, up (+) or down (−) from the table. The curve that strays furthest from zero is the main direction of the movement.
How to read it: it rises when the table starts moving and returns to zero when it stops; the dot marks the maximum velocity. It is computed from the acceleration, so it is an estimate.
How to read it: it is the accumulated distance from the starting point; the dot marks the maximum. It is an estimate: only reliable for short movements (under 1 or 2 s).
Each bar is a measurement, numbered as in the table (oldest on the left). Useful to compare intensities.

For correct measurements:

• Phone FLAT on the table, screen facing up. This keeps the z axis vertical, with x and y lying on the surface: x points to the right of the phone, y toward the top (where the front camera is) and z comes out of the screen.
• Use a firm table, with no tablecloth or pad. A soft surface absorbs the movement.
• The phone must not slide. If it slips, you are measuring its sliding and not the table. You can use double-sided tape or a piece of non-slip rubber.
• Always in the same position and orientation between repetitions, so you can compare. Mark the phone outline with tape.
• No charger plugged in and no dangling cables, since they can pull the phone.
• Do not touch the phone or the table during calibration.
• Avoid outside vibrations: people walking nearby, loud bass music, fans or washing machines. The app would measure them as movement.
• Set the phone to silent with vibration off: the phone own vibration would be measured as movement.
• Use a real phone. The emulator has a simulated accelerometer and does not work.

1. Place the phone as explained above.
2. Tap Calibrate and touch nothing for 2 seconds. The app measures the offset of each axis and the sensor noise. If the high-noise warning appears, repeat the calibration.
3. Adjust the sensitivity if needed. The default value (k = 5) works well in most cases.
4. Tap Measure. The app waits and detects by itself when the movement starts.
5. Move the table (a soft tap, a push, etc.). When the table is still again, the app ends the measurement by itself.
6. Check the result. Type a label (for example strong-x-2) and tap Save.
7. In History you can view, export or delete your measurements.

Repeat each case several times to compare and reduce error.

The largest acceleration value during the movement. It shows how strong the hit or push was at its most intense moment. For reference: 9.8 m/s² equals 1 g (gravity). Below 0.1 m/s² is almost imperceptible; 0.1 to 0.5 is soft; 0.5 to 2 is moderate; 2 to 5 is strong; above 5 is very strong.

The average intensity of the movement over its whole duration. Unlike the peak, it does not depend on a single instant but on the whole event. A sharp hit has a high peak but low RMS; a sustained shake has high RMS. For a sinusoidal signal, RMS = peak / 1.41.

Time from when the acceleration exceeds the threshold until the last time it does. The end is confirmed after 0.3 s of rest. It helps tell a short hit (tenths of a second) from a long movement (several seconds).

The axis with the most movement (highest RMS). x and y are horizontal directions on the table, and z is vertical. If z dominates, the table moved mostly up and down. The RMS and peak of each axis are also shown, in case you want more detail about the direction.

They are computed by integrating the acceleration twice (first velocity, then position). That is why they carry an asterisk: they accumulate error very fast and are only reliable for short movements, under 1 or 2 seconds, with good calibration. Use them as an estimate and compare them with an external measurement (ruler or video). Max displ. is the farthest distance from the starting position and Final displ. is where the table ends up.

Offset is the reading the sensor gives when there is no movement (it should be 0 but almost never is); the app subtracts it from all measurements. Noise is how much the reading fluctuates at rest, usually between 0.01 and 0.05 m/s². Movements smaller than the noise cannot be measured.
The detection threshold is k × noise. A low k detects softer movements but triggers on false vibrations. A high k ignores small vibrations but may miss soft movements. The recommended value is 5.

• Always compare measurements taken with the same phone position and the same calibration.
• If you repeat the same movement and the values are similar, the measurement is reliable. If they change a lot, check that the phone is not sliding and that there are no outside vibrations.
• The stronger the movement, the higher the peak and RMS should be. If not, something is wrong.
• If the peak is very close to the threshold, the movement was almost imperceptible to the sensor and the result is unreliable.
• This app does not replace a professional seismograph: it is a lab tool for studying movement with a phone sensor.

• It does not detect the movement: calibrate again or lower k (move the bar to the left).
• It detects movement without touching anything: raise k, move vibration sources away and calibrate again.
• High-noise warning: something moved during calibration. Repeat it with the table still.
• Different results on each repetition: check that the phone does not slide and is always in the same position.
• Odd velocity and displacement: normal for long movements; trust only the short ones.
